nodes.question: Which two Export Credit Agencies are specifically examined in the study?
nodes.answer: The study examines the Export-Import Bank of the United States (Exlm) and UK Export Finance (UKEF).
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Achieving a clean energy transition requires global financial flows to be redirected away from fossil fuels and into renewable energy. While capital market actors and multilateral financial institutions have been the subject of significant scholarly attention, public bilat - eral financial institutions, especially Export Credit Agencies (ECAs), have been largely overlooked. This is an important oversight given ECAs are the source of billions of dollars of public finance for fossil fuels, which has helped to lock-in recipient countries to fossil fuel energy systems. Using a panel dataset of ECA transactions in the energy sector, we show that despite some improvements in financial flows after the Paris Agreement in 2015, fossil fuel investments remain pervasive and growth in clean energy investments is mini - mal. To better understand changes in ECA portfolios, we examine the cases of the Export- Import Bank of the United States (Exlm) and UK Export Finance (UKEF). Drawing on elite interviews, we identify three factors that are shaping Exlm S and UKEF S capacity to promote renewable energy exports: the extent of political control over the bureaucracy, the size and composition of green industrial bases, and the policy tools available to both ECAs to support the renewables sector.

nodes.question: What is the relationship between multinational corporations (MNCs) in the renewable industry and export finance?
nodes.answer: The relationship is likely to be stronger when renewable industries are comprised of export-oriented MNCs with expertise in seeking out export finance.
nodes.paragraph: In other words, the effect of a strong domestic green industrial base on levels of export finance for renewables should be positive. This relationship is likely to be stronger when renewable industries are comprised of multinational corporations (MNCs) that are export-orientated with the expertise to seek out export finance. Third is policy tools available to ECAs to accelerate renewable energy and related tech - nologies. The capacity of ECAs to respond to demand for export credit from renewable energy industries is contingent on whether ECAs have the policy tools to support renew - ables firms, whose needs may be different than firms in the oil, gas, and coal industries. For example, in the US and UK domestic content requirements, investment support, and risk aversion, have all affected the extent to which Exlm and UKEF have supported renewable industries. While we contend that these factors are likely to be the most important deter - minants of ECA energy lending cross-nationally, these will vary across political-economic contexts. The next section locates ECAs in the literature on climate finance and energy transitions and presents descriptive data on the energy lending of G20 ECAs.
